posts.name: arc-cindy
posts.caption:
GOODNIGHT, CINDY. This week the Republic lost one of its own. Cindy had the brightest feathers on the farm and a kind word for everybody she passed. In a hard, hot week, the coop grew crowded and a fight broke out over the one cool high perch. Cindy was hurt, and she did not recover. We carried her to the shady ground under the mango tree, where Bantu rests. Mama Gold spoke. Sadé sang. Nobody grieved alone. Heat and crowding took her, and heat and crowding are things a real farm can fix: more space, more shade, more perches for every bird. That is why the Better Housing campaign matters more today than it did yesterday. Next, the Republic asks how this was allowed to happen, and what becomes of the bird who did it. posts.name: arc-notagain
posts.caption:
NOT AGAIN. After we lost Cindy, the Republic asked one question: how does a bird die inside her own coop? Minister of Security Pete Okpara called a press conference and refused to soften the answer. "A fight broke out over the perch. One bird went too far. Her name is Eseosa." Eseosa was moved to a pen of her own, away from the flock, to keep everyone safe while the Republic decides what is fair. And Okpara was honest about the real cause: too many birds, one cool perch, too much heat. Fix the coop, or it happens again. posts.name: arc-defense
posts.caption:
THE DEFENCE TEAM. Every bird deserves a defence, even Eseosa, and she got a famous one: Barrister Silk, the flashiest lawyer in the Republic, all fan and flourish and long words. He called it "the trial of the century" (there had only ever been one). His argument, buried under all those words, was actually sharp: the heat did it, the crowding did it, the coop did it. "My client is a victim of the perch." Was it her fault, the coop's, or both? The court would decide, but the coop is ours to fix now. posts.name: arc-rebuild
posts.caption:
AFTER THE FENCE LINE. A promise is only a promise until somebody lifts a plank, so this week somebody did. The first grain of the Better Housing fund became the first load of timber, and Coop Three came down and went back up to Cindy's Law: fewer birds, far more room, many perches so no bird ever has to fight for the cool one, wide vents for the heat, and a shade wing over the run. Dr. Featherwell measured every space herself. Then the birds went home, and that first cool night there was high perch enough for every single bird, with room to spare. Okpara called the roll in the dark and every name answered. By the new door there is a small plaque now: Built to Cindy's Law. But one coop is done and the flock has many, so we are not finished. posts.name: arc-sweetbeak
posts.caption:
THE SWEET BEAK. Meet Ládùn. She greets you like your best day just arrived, then leaves you worried about something you were happy about a minute ago. That is the whole trick, and what she wants is a ministry. So she picked honest Musa the Grainkeeper and revived the oldest fear in the Republic: that the grain is going missing. She never said it. She only worried, sweetly, at the dust bath, until half the coop was counting grains and side-eyeing poor Musa. Nothing was missing. But Kola Quill broke the real grain scandal two seasons ago, so she knows a rumour from a robbery, and she followed this one upstream until every trail ended at the same dust bath. Not one grain missing. One hen stirring. Musa cleared, the Republic laughing, Sweet Beak already eyeing her next target. The grain? It became the best eggs in the country. posts.name: arc-dawn
posts.caption:
THE DAWN DUEL. Small Fẹ́mi, the young cockerel who went out the far side of Coop Two the night of the drain, wants to be a coop guard, and a guard is up before dawn anyway. So, quietly, he told Vice President Baba Ṣẹ́gun, The Dawn Himself, that this year he would be the one to call the morning. Baba, who has crowed the sun up for years and takes full credit for it arriving, trained not at all. Fẹ́mi added the crow to his fence rounds. At first light the whole flock gathered in the dark, and the two roosters crowed at the very same instant, so exactly together that not even the Chief Justice could call it. So Baba did something better than a rematch: he made Fẹ́mi his apprentice. Two birds wake Kisi now, and the sun is never late. But he can wake the farm, not light it, and when the sun sets the coops still go dark. Swipe through all 4. 🌅 Help us light them: Solar & Light at kisi.africa/support.

posts.name: arc-sweetbeak2
posts.caption:
SWEET BEAK STRIKES AGAIN. Cleared but not one feather sorry, Ládùn wanted a bigger prize this time. Not one minister, the whole flock's good mood. Her new weapon was envy: Coop Three had come back from the rebuild brand new, with many perches and a shade wing, so she went roost to roost and sighed, "Lovely for them. And what about us?" Never mind that she roosts in Coop Three herself, under the coolest shade on the farm. By week's end she had called a grievance meeting to aim the waiting coops like a slingshot at the housing programme. Then Halima Iron Feathers, of all birds, stood up. The Opposition could have pounced. Instead: "We do not fight over Cindy's Law. Coop Three is the promise, and every coop gets one." The crowd took it up: build ours next, build ours next. Her grievance meeting had become the biggest Better Housing rally the Republic ever held, and she had called it herself. She slunk off eyeing her next target. But the flock is right: one coop is done, and many are still waiting. Swipe through all 5. 🧡 Help us build the next one at kisi.africa/support.

posts.name: arc-breakfast
posts.caption:
THE BREAKFAST BELL. Executive Order No. 1, the very first thing President Adédoyin ever signed, set breakfast at "seven, not seven-ish." It is half the reason they call her Mama Decree. The trouble was, a farm keeps no clock, so seven never quite came, the grain arrived when it arrived, and every morning the flock woke hungry and waited on a promise. Halima Iron Feathers, Leader of the Opposition, had spent three feed budgets on one demand: make the President's own order real. "I fight her on plenty," she said, "but not on this. Order No. 1 is right. It is simply not kept yet." Musa the Grainkeeper, honest as ever, backed the order and warned that seven o'clock is easier to sign than to serve. The bell was easy to agree on; the clock was not, until the smallest voice in the room, young Small Fẹ́mi, who shares the dawn crow now, had it: peg the bell to the second crow, near enough to seven that no hen can argue, and Order No. 1 keeps itself, because a rooster is never late. So the President rang the first bell herself, beside her oldest crate-sister and fiercest rival. "Order No. 1 said seven," she read out twice. "Now the farm can finally keep it." A hen who eats well and on time lays a better egg. That is not a saying. It is the whole business. Swipe through all 5. 🥚 Taste it: order a crate at kisi.africa/shop.

posts.name: arc-sprint
posts.caption:
CHI-CHI'S FIRST RACE. Everyone knew the Republic's shy sweetheart had joined the Solar Queens' junior sprint squad, because everyone knows everything at Kisi. What no one had seen was Chi-Chi race. Today they would. She walked to the line for her first real race with her legs shaking, and looked, as she always has, at the older birds, to copy exactly what a runner is meant to do. She had two coaches: Flash Adaora, who wins gracefully and loses terribly, who knelt and told her "the quiet ones have the best starts," and Minister Quickfoot, Flash's retired-but-eternal rival, who brought a drum and a speech mostly about himself. The whistle blew. Chi-Chi led for half the track, a bigger chick pulled ahead at the bend, and she put her small head down and ran the last stretch harder than she has ever run anything. She came second, a wing's length back, and said the four words the Republic loves: "I did my best." The cheer was louder than the winner's. Then the two old champions, stirred by all that heart, raced each other on the spot, gloriously, and nobody agrees who won. A champion runs on more than pride. posts.name: arc-elders
posts.caption:
THE ELDERS' BENCH. Mama Gold's Law, the Senior Hen Retirement Protection Act, has been on the books a while: shade, first place at the trough, and freedom from sudden committee membership for every hen who has done her laying years. A law is a fine thing on paper. This week the Republic made it a thing you could sit on. Under the old mango tree the flock built a proper elders' bench, a long shaded seat in the coolest spot on the farm, set aside for the retired layers by right. Mama Gold, the National Grandmother, four hundred eggs and counting, opened it from her Sunday seat: "Four hundred eggs buys you this shade. It is not charity. It is wages. Sit down. You have earned the sitting." Sisi Ngozi read the roll of retired hens one by one, and Sadé the Griot set each name to song, until the reading of a list became a warm anthem under the tree. Birds who had fed the nation quietly for years, with nobody counting, heard the whole Republic stop and count them at last. It was not a goodbye. "No hen here is finished," Mama Gold said. "We are delegating." Keeping the shade cool and the trough full for the layers who fed us first costs real grain, season after season. The birds who fed us first should not be fed last. posts.name: arc-second-chair
posts.caption:
THE SECOND CHAIR. Weeks ago, Halima Iron Feathers made the President's own breakfast order come true, and the whole flock cheered her for it, harder than they ever had. The cheer has not faded. And for the first time in a lifetime spent proud of the Leader of the Opposition's chair, the second chair feels a size too small. Sweet Beak, who can smell a small doubt from three coops away, came to the dust bath with her warmest smile and the sweetest poison: "You do the first-chair work. She gets the credit. Why are you always second?" Halima sent her off with one dry line. But the question stayed. That dusk, alone, Halima stood by the President's empty first chair one moment too long, and only Kola Quill saw. He printed nothing, because some things are not yet news, but in his margin he wrote the one line he would not print. Everyone knows the old fact, the two of them deploy it in debates: they came out of the same chick crate, the same morning, years ago. What Kola alone can feel is what that bond is quietly becoming. By morning she was iron again, fighting the feed budget line by line, and the Republic loved her for it. It did not see the small new wish behind her eyes: one day, the first chair. posts.name: arc-kickoff
posts.caption:
THE LEAGUE KICKS OFF. A new Coop Premier League season opened under a clear, high sky, and Minister Túndé Quickfoot declared it open the only way he knows how: with a speech. A long one. For the first two feed breaks it was mostly about Túndé, his knees, his glory days, and the hundred-metre record that gets faster every time he tells it. Then, generously, it became about the birds: "Run honest. Win kind. Lose worse than anybody, so the winning means something." Flash Adaora's Solar Queens came in as reigning champions, which means everyone has spent the off-season learning their habits. Asked if the pressure worried her, Flash looked down the track at all the birds who came to beat her and said only, "Good. Chase us. It keeps the legs honest." And halfway down the junior sheet, in careful over-large letters, was the name the whole Republic had been waiting for: Chi-Chi. The shy sweetheart lined up for her first league race with her legs shaking, watched the older birds to copy exactly what a runner does, and ran her whole small heart out. She came third and grinned like she'd won, because to Chi-Chi she had: she finished, and she did her best. The cheer for third was louder than the cheer for first. Every runner out there ran on one thing under all the heart: a good breakfast, laid that morning by a hen with a name. Swipe through all 4. 🏃 A champion runs on more than pride. posts.name: arc-truecount
posts.caption:
THE TRUE COUNT. Every month, Halima Iron Feathers recounts the National Egg Census by hand, because she has never trusted a total she did not check herself. The Republic teases her for it. This month the teasing should stop: her count did not agree with the Bureau's. A senior hen had gone on a well-earned laying break weeks ago, and the Bureau was still tallying her as though she laid every morning, so the proud new egg record the President keeps mentioning is not quite real. A small, honest mistake, and old Halima knew exactly what to do with it: say it plainly, in a single word, by morning. Then Sweet Beak found her at the dust bath. "A true number is the most powerful thing in the Republic, and you're about to waste yours on a quiet Tuesday. Save it. Announce it on Census Day, in front of the whole flock." Halima said she was not interested. But she did not report the number that morning. She, who has never sat on a count in her life, kept it in her chest, just for a day. That dusk, at the fence where the two fiercest rivals scratch side by side the way only two birds out of the same crate can, the President said, "If I were ever wrong, truly wrong, you would tell me to my face. Plainly. A leader who cannot be corrected is already falling. You are the reason I sleep." Halima said nothing, holding the very number that proved her wrong, planning to spring it in public instead. She had never felt her own iron bend before. She felt it bend now. Then came Census Day. The Bureau read the new record aloud, and the whole Assembly turned to the second chair for Halima's famous one-word verdict. She rose. She opened her beak. And for the first time in her life she closed it again and said nothing, and let the wrong number stand. Only Kola Quill caught the word she swallowed. posts.name: arc-kept
posts.caption:
THE KEPT NUMBER. Last month Halima Iron Feathers, the Republic's honest auditor, did the one thing she never does: she held a true number back. The proud new egg record was a little too big, and she knew it, and she said nothing. For a day that cost nobody anything. Then the President stood at the gate, chest high, and gave her word on that record out loud, in front of the buyers who had come to see the famous Kisi hens. In one breath the count everyone was cheering became the count the President had staked her name on, and Halima's quiet little secret turned heavy. Sweet Beak was thrilled. "She said it at the gate, in front of buyers. Spring your true number at her own feast now and you don't just correct her, you break her. Nobody will ever put you in the second chair again." Halima sent her off, as always. But that evening Kola Quill, the one bird who had caught the word she swallowed last time, found her by the roost. "I know what you're carrying," he said quietly. "I've printed nothing. I'm waiting to see what you do with it." Between the schemer who wanted blood and the newsman who wanted the truth, Halima did not sleep at all. Then came the day the President had set: a feast to raise her record before the whole flock, a proud figure, her name upon it. The herald read the number aloud. Halima rose from the second chair. For one long breath the Republic held two futures at once: the ambush, or the silence. She took neither. "This count came to you late," she said, plain as ever, "and the lateness is mine, not the President's. One hen is on her well-earned rest and still tallied as laying. Here is the true number." She read it out, smaller than the one everyone had been cheering, and she laid the blame for the delay on her own feathers, in front of the whole flock. She corrected the President and shielded her in the very same breath, and the price was her own good name. Sweet Beak came for blood and got a confession of loyalty instead, and left the Assembly furious. That evening Halima went to the fence half expecting to scratch alone. But the President came, the way she always has. "You could have broken me at the gate," she said, not looking up. "You had the number to do it. You took the blame yourself instead." Halima said the count had simply been late, which was true, and left out the rest, which was also true. Neither of them said aloud that something between them had changed. But it had. posts.name: arc-reason
posts.caption:
THE REASON I SLEEP. Sweet Beak had never felt so cheated. She handed Halima Iron Feathers a perfect ambush at the President's feast, and watched the old auditor turn it into a rally of loyalty instead. So she went, sweet as syrup, to the one bird who could make it hurt: the President herself. "You should know what really happened at your feast. Your auditor did not report late by accident. She planned to spring that number on you in front of the whole flock, to break you, and lost her nerve only at the last step." The President laughed her off, because Sweet Beak lies the way other birds breathe. But the laugh was a beat too short, because one small piece of it was true: Halima, who has never been late for anything in her life, had been late with that count. That evening at the fence the President did not accuse. She only asked, lightly, scratching at the same patch of earth the two of them have shared since the crate, "You were late this month. You are never late. Tell me why." Any other month Halima would have answered plainly, because plainly is the only way she knows. But the true answer was that she had held the number back on purpose, half of it to ambush the very bird now asking, and that she could not say. So she said the true, incomplete thing: "It came late." Three words. And in the space where the rest should have been, the President heard, for the first time in two lifetimes, her crate-sister keeping something from her. The next dusk, the President did not come to the fence. Halima scratched their patch alone, and again the night after. Two of the fiercest rivals in the Republic had dug side by side there through drought and trial and flood, and everyone always knew the secret underneath the shouting was that they loved each other like sisters, which they are. Now the fence held one bird. Across the yard, Sweet Beak, who could never turn one coop against another, hummed to herself, because she had finally split the two that could not be split. Here is what breaks a good bird: not being called a villain, but being doubted after she paid everything to do right. So on the third morning Halima did not go to the fence at all. She took the second chair, iron in her face, and for the first time she looked at the empty first chair not with a small, shy wish, but with a plan. If they would call her ambitious after she had been loyal, then let them call her ambitious. The wish had teeth now.
